metadata.title: English Reading Comprehension Texts by CEFR Level
metadata.description: 60 texts (10 per level) with 5 to 10 comprehension questions each. Text length, vocabulary, genre, number of questions, number of options, question skills and hints are calibrated to each CEFR level.
metadata.framework: CEFR (Common European Framework of Reference for Languages)

level_settings.options: Number of options in multiple-choice questions.
level_settings.hint: "sentence" highlights the sentence with the answer, "paragraph" highlights its paragraph, "none" has no hint.

text_fields.description: Short summary with the topic keywords (used on the cards and in the hub search).

question_fields.type: "mc" (multiple choice), "tf" (true / false) or "tfng" (true / false / not given).
question_fields.skill: main idea, detail, vocabulary, inference, reference, purpose or tone.
question_fields.q: The question, or the statement for tf and tfng.
question_fields.options: mc only: the FIRST option is the correct one. The game shuffles the options.
question_fields.answer: tf and tfng only: "true", "false" or "not given".
question_fields.quote: Exact words from the text that support the answer (highlighted after answering and used by the hint).

puzzles.description: A boy's daily routine, from breakfast to bedtime: school, homework and free time.
text: Hi! My name is Lucas and I am twelve years old. I live in Curitiba with my mother and my little sister, Bia.
I get up at half past six every day. I have breakfast with my sister, usually bread and milk. Then I walk to school. It is only ten minutes from my house.
School finishes at twelve thirty. In the afternoon, I do my homework and play football with my friends in the park.
We have dinner at seven. After dinner, I read a book or watch TV. I go to bed at nine thirty, but on Saturdays I go to bed late!

puzzles.description: An email about a weekend trip to Rio de Janeiro: travel by bus, sightseeing and rainy weather.
text: Hi Tom,

I'm back from Rio de Janeiro! I went there last weekend with my cousin Mariana. We took the bus on Friday night and arrived early on Saturday morning. The trip was long, about six hours, but we slept most of the time.

On Saturday, the weather was perfect. We visited Sugarloaf Mountain in the morning and went to Copacabana Beach in the afternoon. The view from the mountain was amazing, but it was very crowded. We also tried açaí for the first time.
Unfortunately, it rained all day on Sunday, so we couldn't go to the Christ the Redeemer statue. Instead, we went to a museum and had lunch in a nice Italian restaurant.
I spent more money than I planned, but it was a great weekend. Next time, I want to stay for a whole week!
See you soon,
Camila

puzzles.description: Magazine tips for a healthier lifestyle and wellbeing: water, walking, breakfast, sleep and phones.
text: Do you want to feel better and have more energy? You don't need to change your whole life. Try these five simple habits.
1. Drink more water. Many people drink only when they feel thirsty. Carry a bottle with you and try to drink about two litres a day.
2. Walk more. You don't have to go to the gym. Take the stairs instead of the lift, or get off the bus one stop early.
3. Eat breakfast. People who eat a good breakfast usually eat less junk food later in the day. Fruit, eggs and oats are great choices.
4. Go to bed at the same time every night. Adults need seven to nine hours of sleep.
5. Turn off your phone an hour before bed. The light from screens makes it harder to fall asleep. Read a book instead.

puzzles.description: A blog post about a first summer job in an ice cream shop and what work taught the writer.
text: When I was seventeen, I got my first job. I worked in an ice cream shop in my town during the summer holidays. I wanted to save money for a new laptop.

The job was harder than I expected. I started at two o'clock and finished at ten, six days a week. I served customers, cleaned the tables and washed a lot of dishes. On hot days, there was a long queue outside the shop, and I never had time to sit down.
My boss, Mr Rossi, was strict but fair. He taught me to smile at every customer, even the rude ones. I made some mistakes at the beginning, but after two weeks I was much faster.

At the end of the summer, I had enough money for my laptop. But the best thing was not the money. I learned to work in a team and to be responsible. And now I can't eat ice cream without thinking about that summer!

text: Last July, my friends and I went to Sunset Fest, a three-day music festival near the coast. We bought the tickets in January because they always sell out quickly.
We stayed in a small tent in the camping area. On the first night, it rained a lot and our tent was wet in the morning, so we slept in my friend Carla's car the next night!

The music was fantastic. My favourite band played on Saturday evening, and thousands of people sang every song with them. On Sunday, we discovered a young singer from Chile. I didn't know her before, but now I listen to her every day.
The food was quite expensive, so we cooked pasta at the campsite. It wasn't delicious, but it was cheap.
I was very tired when I got home, but I want to go again next year.

text: Last year, Marcos, a 34-year-old teacher, received a text message that seemed to come from his bank. It said there was a problem with his account and asked him to click on a link. Experts say a few simple habits can protect you. Never click on links in unexpected messages; instead, open your bank's app or call the number on your card. Be suspicious of offers that seem too good to be true. And if a message says you must act immediately, stop and take a breath: that pressure is usually a warning sign. puzzles.description: An article about remote work and the hybrid model: flexibility, productivity, loneliness and the future of the office.
text: Before 2020, working from home was a privilege enjoyed by a small minority, mostly freelancers and tech workers. Then the pandemic forced millions of employees to set up offices on kitchen tables almost overnight. Years later, many of them have no intention of going back.

For supporters, the advantages are obvious. Without a daily commute, workers save time and money, and many say they can concentrate better away from noisy open-plan offices. Companies benefit too: they can hire talented people who live far away and spend less on expensive office space.

However, the picture is not entirely positive. Several studies suggest that remote workers find it harder to switch off, often answering emails late at night. Loneliness is another common complaint, particularly among young employees who live alone. Managers, meanwhile, worry that creativity suffers when colleagues no longer bump into each other in corridors, and that new staff struggle to learn from more experienced colleagues.

As a result, a compromise has become increasingly popular. Under the hybrid model, employees spend two or three days in the office and work from home for the rest of the week. In theory, this combines the best of both worlds. In practice, it only works when teams agree on which days to come in; otherwise, people travel to the office only to spend the day on video calls.

What seems certain is that the traditional nine-to-five office week is unlikely to return for good. Some large companies have tried to order employees back five days a week, but many have faced resistance, and some have lost valuable staff to more flexible competitors. The question now is not whether people will work remotely, but how organisations can make it work fairly for everyone.

puzzles.theme: The Hidden Cost of Fast Fashion
puzzles.description: An article about fast fashion and the environment: cheap clothes, water use, textile waste, recycling and sustainable shopping.
text: A T-shirt for the price of a sandwich sounds like a bargain. But according to environmental groups, the true cost of cheap clothing is paid elsewhere: in polluted rivers, overflowing landfills and factories where workers earn barely enough to survive.

Fast fashion brands have transformed the industry by producing new collections every few weeks instead of twice a year. As a result, global clothing production roughly doubled between 2000 and 2015, while the number of times an item is worn before being thrown away fell by around a third. Low prices encourage shoppers to buy on impulse, often for a single occasion, and many garments are designed to last only a few washes.

The environmental impact is enormous. Producing a single pair of jeans can require several thousand litres of water, much of it used to grow cotton. Synthetic fabrics such as polyester, which are made from oil, release tiny plastic fibres every time they are washed, and these eventually reach the oceans. Meanwhile, the equivalent of a rubbish truck full of textiles is burned or buried every second.

Some brands have responded with recycling schemes and “conscious” collections. Critics, however, argue that these initiatives are largely marketing. Only a tiny percentage of collected clothing is actually turned into new garments, since mixed fabrics are extremely difficult to separate. In many cases, donated clothes are shipped to countries in Africa and Asia, where large amounts end up in local landfills.

Real change, experts say, depends less on recycling and more on buying fewer, better-made clothes. Second-hand shopping, clothing swaps and repairing damaged items are all growing trends, especially among young consumers. Governments are also starting to act: France, for example, has banned companies from destroying unsold goods. The most sustainable piece of clothing, as one designer put it, is the one already hanging in your wardrobe.

puzzles.description: A psychology article about procrastination: emotions, stress, deadlines and strategies to stop putting things off.
text: You sit down to write a report that is due tomorrow. Twenty minutes later, you have checked the news, reorganised your desk and watched three videos about cats. Sound familiar? You are not alone: studies suggest that around 20% of adults are chronic procrastinators, and the figure is far higher among university students.

For decades, procrastination was seen as a problem of laziness or poor time management. Today, many psychologists see it differently. According to Dr Tim Pychyl, who has studied the subject for more than twenty years, procrastination is mainly an emotional problem. We delay tasks that make us feel bored, anxious or insecure, because avoiding them brings immediate relief. The trouble is that the relief doesn't last, and the task, along with the stress, is still waiting for us later.

This explains why simply buying a new planner rarely helps. If the real cause is a negative feeling, the solution has to address that feeling. One effective strategy is to make the first step so small that it seems almost ridiculous: instead of “write the report”, the goal becomes “open the document and write one sentence”. Once people start, they usually continue.

Another technique is to be kinder to yourself. Surprisingly, research with students has shown that those who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam procrastinated less before the next one. Harsh self-criticism, it seems, only adds to the negative emotions that caused the delay in the first place.

Deadlines can also help, but only if they are specific. Promising to “start next week” is easy to break; deciding to work “on Tuesday at 9 a.m. in the library” is much harder to ignore. Telling a friend about your plan makes it even more likely that you will stick to it.

puzzles.description: A restaurant review: food, dishes, service, price and atmosphere at a new restaurant in São Paulo.
text: When The Glass Garden opened in a converted greenhouse in São Paulo's Pinheiros district last spring, the city's food lovers could hardly contain their excitement. Its chef, Marina Okada, had spent a decade in some of Europe's most celebrated kitchens, and the restaurant promised “seasonal Brazilian cooking with a Japanese soul”. Six months on, I finally managed to get a table. Was it worth the three-week wait?

The setting certainly is. Diners sit among lemon trees and hanging herbs under a glass roof, and at sunset the room glows. It is, however, remarkably loud. On a busy Friday night, my companion and I had to lean across the table to hear each other. The tables are also very close together, which some diners may find uncomfortable.

The food, for the most part, lives up to the hype. A starter of grilled heart of palm with miso butter was simply outstanding: smoky, rich and perfectly balanced. The main course, fish cooked in banana leaves with a ginger and cashew sauce, was equally impressive, although the portion was small for the price. Only the dessert disappointed. A passion fruit mousse looked beautiful but tasted oddly of nothing.

Service was friendly and knowledgeable, if a little slow. Our waiter explained each dish with obvious enthusiasm, but we waited almost forty minutes between courses, and nobody apologised. Tables near the kitchen seemed to be served much faster than ours.

At around R$ 280 per person without drinks, The Glass Garden is not an everyday option. Yet for a special occasion, it offers something genuinely original. Book well in advance, avoid Friday nights if you want a conversation, and whatever you do, don't skip the heart of palm.
Rating: 4 out of 5

puzzles.description: An opinion piece about overtourism: travel, local communities, housing and holiday rentals, and responsible tourism.
text: Every summer, the residents of certain European cities brace themselves. In Barcelona, Venice and Amsterdam, visitors now outnumber locals by enormous margins, and the frustration has become impossible to ignore. Protesters have sprayed tourists with water pistols, and walls are covered in messages telling visitors to go home. It is tempting to dismiss this as simple hostility. It isn't.

Tourism brings money and jobs, and many towns depend on it. The problem is not tourism itself but its concentration. When millions of people want to see the same bridge or square during the same few weeks, daily life becomes almost impossible for those who live nearby. Pavements are blocked, local shops are replaced by souvenir stores, and a trip to the supermarket turns into an obstacle course.

Housing is perhaps the most serious issue. As property owners discover they can earn far more by renting to tourists through online platforms than to long-term tenants, rents rise and residents are pushed out. In some historic centres, whole buildings now contain no permanent residents at all. A neighbourhood without neighbours, however picturesque, is little more than a theme park.

Some cities are fighting back. Venice has introduced an entry fee for day-trippers on busy days, while Amsterdam has restricted holiday rentals and banned new hotels in its centre. Critics argue that such measures punish ordinary travellers and hurt small businesses, and they may have a point. Yet doing nothing is clearly no longer an option.

Travellers, too, can make a difference. Visiting in the low season, staying longer in one place, choosing lesser-known destinations and spending money in locally owned businesses all help to spread the benefits of tourism more fairly. The goal should not be fewer journeys, but more thoughtful ones.

puzzles.description: A science article about sleep, memory and learning: what the brain does at night, studying for exams and health.
text: For a long time, sleep was thought of as a passive state, a kind of pause button for the body and the brain. Research over the past few decades has overturned that idea. While we sleep, the brain is extraordinarily busy, and one of its most important jobs is processing what we learned during the day.

During the day, new information is stored temporarily in the hippocampus, a small region deep inside the brain. At night, particularly during deep sleep, these memories are replayed and gradually transferred to the cortex, where they can be kept for the long term. Scientists often compare the process to moving files from a computer's desktop into organised folders.

The evidence for this is striking. In one well-known experiment, participants learned a list of word pairs in the evening. Those who slept normally remembered significantly more the next morning than those who were kept awake, even when both groups were allowed to sleep the following night. The lost sleep, it seems, could not simply be made up later.

Sleep also appears to help us see connections that we missed while awake. In another study, people who slept after working on a mathematical problem were more than twice as likely to discover a hidden shortcut as those who stayed awake. Scientists believe this happens because the sleeping brain reorganises information and combines it in new ways.

This has clear implications for students. Staying up all night before an exam may feel productive, but it undermines the very process that makes studying effective. Experts recommend spreading revision over several days and protecting sleep, especially the night after learning something new. As one researcher put it, sleep is not the enemy of studying; it is part of it.

options: Sleep plays an active role in memory and problem-solving

Students should do most of their studying at night

puzzles.theme: The Gig Economy: Freedom or Trap?
puzzles.description: An article about the gig economy: work through apps, delivery drivers, flexibility, workers' rights and income.
text: Open any delivery app in a big city and, within minutes, someone on a motorbike will bring you dinner. Behind that convenience is a way of working that has grown rapidly over the past decade: the gig economy, in which people are paid per task, or “gig”, rather than receiving a regular salary.

For many workers, the attraction is flexibility. Drivers and couriers can decide when and how long to work, which suits students, parents and people who want to earn extra money alongside another job. Getting started is also quick: in most cases, all you need is a phone, a vehicle and a few documents.

Critics, however, argue that this freedom is often an illusion. Because gig workers are usually classified as independent contractors rather than employees, they generally have no paid holidays, sick pay or pension contributions. If they have an accident while working, they may lose their income entirely. Moreover, the apps decide how much each task pays, and rates can change overnight without any negotiation.

Many workers also describe a sense of being controlled by algorithms. Couriers who reject too many orders may receive fewer offers afterwards, which puts pressure on them to accept badly paid trips. As one delivery rider in São Paulo put it: “They say I'm my own boss, but the app is the one giving the orders.”

Governments are starting to respond. Spain, for example, passed a law in 2021 that presumes delivery riders working through apps are employees, and courts in several other countries have reached similar decisions. The companies, for their part, warn that stricter rules could raise prices for customers and reduce the number of jobs available. The debate is far from over, but it raises a question that will shape the future of work: can flexibility and security go together?

Gig workers earn more than employees

puzzles.description: An article about the return of vinyl records: music, streaming technology, nostalgia, artists and young consumers.
text: In the early 2000s, vinyl records seemed destined for museums. CDs had replaced them years before, and digital downloads were about to replace CDs. Yet today, record shops are opening again in cities around the world, and vinyl sales have grown for well over a decade. In some countries, they now earn more money than CDs.

Surprisingly, much of this growth is driven not by older collectors but by young people, many of whom listen to most of their music on streaming platforms. So why would someone who can access millions of songs on their phone pay for a heavy, fragile disc?

Part of the answer is that streaming has made music almost invisible. Songs play in the background while we work or travel, and it is easy to skip a track after a few seconds. A record, by contrast, demands attention. You have to choose it, place it on the turntable and turn it over halfway through. For many fans, this ritual makes listening feel intentional rather than automatic.

Ownership matters too. When a streaming service removes an album, it simply disappears from your library. A record, on the other hand, is a physical object with large artwork and printed lyrics, something you can display on a shelf or give as a gift. For artists, especially independent ones, selling records at concerts has also become an important source of income, since streaming pays very little per play.

Not everyone is convinced. Some audio experts point out that digital files can reproduce sound just as accurately, and that the ‘warmth’ people love in vinyl partly comes from small imperfections. Records are also expensive and, being made of plastic, not especially environmentally friendly. Still, for a generation raised on screens, vinyl offers something that no algorithm can: the pleasure of holding music in your hands.

puzzles.description: A science article about the placebo effect: medicine, health, pain, the brain and the way doctors talk to patients.
text: In medical trials, some patients receive a real drug while others, without knowing it, are given a placebo: a sugar pill with no active ingredient. Researchers expect the drug to perform better. What surprises many people is how often patients taking the placebo also report feeling better.

This phenomenon, known as the placebo effect, is not simply imagination. Brain scans have shown that when people expect pain relief, their brains can release natural painkillers called endorphins. Expectations appear to influence symptoms that depend heavily on the brain, such as pain, nausea, tiredness and anxiety. However, a placebo cannot shrink a tumour or cure an infection, and it would be dangerous to suggest otherwise.

The details of the treatment matter remarkably. Studies have found that two placebo pills tend to work better than one, and that injections often have stronger effects than pills. Even the colour can make a difference: in some experiments, blue pills were more effective as sleeping aids, while red ones seemed better at increasing energy. The price counts, too. People who were told a pill was expensive reported more relief than those who believed it was cheap.

Perhaps most surprising is the so-called open-label placebo. In several small studies, patients with conditions such as chronic back pain were told honestly that they were taking sugar pills, yet many still reported improvements. Researchers believe the ritual of taking medicine, combined with care and attention from a doctor, may be enough to trigger a response.

The opposite effect also exists. When patients are warned about possible side effects, some begin to experience them even if they are taking a placebo. This “nocebo” effect shows that the way doctors communicate is not just a matter of politeness; it can directly affect how patients feel.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the article?
options: Expectations can have real effects on how patients feel

Doctors should stop prescribing real medicine
Expensive medicine is always more effective
questions.explain: The article shows how expectations, details of treatment and communication affect symptoms, within clear limits.

puzzles.description: An article about fake news and misinformation: social media, the news, technology, emotions and how to check information.
text: A few years ago, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology analysed around 126,000 stories shared on Twitter over more than a decade. Their conclusion was alarming: false news spread significantly faster, further and deeper than true news. False stories were about 70% more likely to be shared than accurate ones.

Surprisingly, automated accounts, or bots, were not the main reason. They spread true and false stories at roughly the same rate. It was humans who were responsible for the difference. The researchers suggested that false news tends to be more novel, and novelty attracts attention. People enjoy being the first to share surprising information, which can make them look well informed.

Emotions play a central role as well. Stories that provoke anger, fear or disgust are more likely to go viral, because strong feelings push us to react quickly rather than think carefully. Headlines are often written specifically to trigger these reactions. Social media platforms make this worse: their algorithms tend to promote content that generates engagement, and outrage is extremely engaging.

Fortunately, there are ways to slow the spread. Studies suggest that simply prompting people to think about accuracy before sharing makes them less likely to pass on false headlines. Some educators also recommend “lateral reading”: instead of staying on a suspicious website, open new tabs and check what other reliable sources say about it. Professional fact-checkers do this routinely, and it takes less than a minute.

Nobody is completely immune to misinformation, including highly educated people. In fact, confidence in our own judgement can make us less careful. The most useful habit may be the simplest one: when a story makes you feel a strong emotion, pause before sharing it. That moment of hesitation could stop a lie from reaching thousands of people.

To prove that bots create most fake news
To persuade people to leave social media

puzzles.description: A psychology article about multitasking, attention and focus at work: task switching, distraction and productivity.
text: Few boasts are as common in job interviews as the claim to be an excellent multitasker. In a world of constant notifications, the ability to write a report, answer messages and follow a video meeting at the same time sounds not only useful but essential. There is just one problem: according to decades of cognitive research, what most of us call multitasking barely exists.

When we believe we are doing two demanding things at once, the brain is in fact switching rapidly between them. Each switch carries a cost. The mind has to disengage from one set of rules and goals and load another, a process that takes only fractions of a second but adds up quickly. Some estimates suggest that switching between tasks can consume as much as 40% of a person's productive time. Errors increase too, particularly when the tasks are similar, such as listening to one conversation while reading an unrelated email.

Perhaps more worrying is what habitual multitasking seems to do to our ability to focus. In a frequently cited Stanford study, heavy media multitaskers performed worse than light multitaskers on tests requiring them to ignore irrelevant information. Ironically, the people who multitasked most were the least skilled at it. The researchers could not establish whether multitasking caused the weakness or whether easily distracted people are simply drawn to it, but the finding has been widely discussed.

There are genuine exceptions. We can walk and talk, or listen to music while cooking, because one of the activities is so well practised that it requires little conscious attention. The trouble begins when both tasks compete for the same mental resources. That is why using a hands-free phone while driving remains dangerous: the hands may be free, but the mind is not.

None of this means that modern workers can simply ignore their inboxes. It does suggest, however, that the way many workplaces are organised is counterproductive. Some companies have begun experimenting with “focus hours” in which meetings and messages are banned, and early reports are encouraging. For individuals, the advice is refreshingly simple: do one thing at a time, turn off notifications while working on something important, and deal with messages in batches rather than as they arrive. It may feel slower. The evidence suggests it is anything but.

options: What we call multitasking is largely an illusion that harms performance
Multitasking is an essential modern skill that can be trained
Technology has made people better at concentrating
Companies should ban all messages during working hours

puzzles.description: An article about urban planning: cities designed for cars, traffic and induced demand, parking, pollution and car-free streets.
text: For much of the twentieth century, urban planners shared a clear vision of progress: wide avenues, elevated highways and generous parking, all designed to move cars as quickly as possible. Cities from Los Angeles to São Paulo were reshaped around this ideal, sometimes demolishing entire neighbourhoods to make room for roads. Today, a growing number of planners regard that vision as one of the costliest mistakes of the modern era.

The central problem is a phenomenon known as induced demand. When a congested road is widened, traffic initially flows more freely, which makes driving more attractive. People who previously took the bus, travelled at different times or avoided the journey altogether begin to drive, and within a few years the new lanes are as jammed as the old ones. Houston's Katy Freeway, expanded to as many as 26 lanes in places at a cost of nearly three billion dollars, is a frequently cited example: journey times at peak hours actually increased after the work was completed.

Car-centred design also has less obvious costs. Parking consumes vast amounts of valuable land; in some American cities, it covers more space than all the buildings combined. Wide, fast roads divide communities and discourage walking, which in turn contributes to sedentary lifestyles. Air pollution from traffic, meanwhile, is linked to thousands of premature deaths every year. And because such cities spread outwards, services become more expensive to provide and people without cars, often the poorest residents, are left with few options.

The alternative is not to abolish cars but to stop giving them priority by default. Paris has converted riverside expressways into parks and added hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes. Seoul demolished an elevated highway and restored the stream that ran beneath it, creating a popular public space. Barcelona's “superblocks” group several city blocks together and restrict through traffic, turning former streets into squares and playgrounds.

Such changes are rarely popular at first. Shop owners fear losing customers, and drivers protest loudly. Yet studies of pedestrianised streets often show that retail sales rise rather than fall, as people on foot tend to linger and return more often. Once the benefits become visible, opposition tends to fade. The lesson may be that cities, like roads, fill up with whatever they are designed for.

puzzles.description: An essay about technology and privacy: personal data, the internet, consent, data protection laws and power.
text: Every time you search for a restaurant, accept a cookie or walk past a shop with your phone in your pocket, you leave a trace. Individually, these fragments of information seem trivial. Combined and analysed, they can reveal where you live and work, what you earn, whether you are pregnant or unwell, and even how you are likely to vote. This detailed picture has become one of the most valuable commodities of the digital economy, yet the people it describes rarely see any of the profits.

Technology companies generally defend their practices by pointing out that users agree to them. Technically, this is true. In practice, the consent is largely a fiction. Privacy policies are notoriously long and vague; one study calculated that reading every policy an average internet user encounters in a year would take around 76 working days. Faced with a choice between accepting the terms or being unable to use a service that friends, employers and schools rely on, most people click “agree” without a second thought.

Regulators have begun to respond. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which came into force in 2018, requires companies to explain clearly what data they collect and allows citizens to request copies of it or ask for it to be deleted. Brazil's own data protection law, the LGPD, was heavily inspired by the European model. Fines under these laws can be substantial, and several technology giants have already paid hundreds of millions of euros.

Critics, however, argue that such rules treat the symptoms rather than the cause. If a business model depends on collecting as much information as possible, they say, companies will always find creative ways to obtain consent. Some economists have proposed a radical alternative: treating personal data as a form of property, so that individuals could sell or license it. Others warn that this would simply allow the poor to sell their privacy cheaply, turning a fundamental right into a luxury.

What is clear is that the question can no longer be left to engineers and lawyers alone. Most people would never allow a stranger to follow them around all day taking notes, yet online, something very similar happens constantly. Data now shapes the prices we are offered, the news we read and, increasingly, the decisions made about our loans, jobs and health care. Deciding who controls it is, in the end, a question about power.

puzzles.description: An article about loneliness and social isolation as a public health issue: causes in modern society, mental health and community solutions.
text: In 2018, the United Kingdom did something no country had done before: it appointed a minister for loneliness. The decision was greeted with some amusement abroad, but it reflected a growing body of evidence that social isolation is not merely an unpleasant feeling but a serious public health issue. Some researchers have gone as far as to claim that chronic loneliness is as harmful to health as smoking fifteen cigarettes a day, although that particular comparison has been questioned.

What is less disputed is that loneliness affects the body in measurable ways. People who feel isolated for long periods tend to have higher levels of stress hormones, weaker immune responses and poorer sleep. They face an increased risk of heart disease, depression and, in older age, dementia. Evolutionary psychologists suggest a reason: for most of human history, being separated from the group meant danger, so the brain learned to treat isolation as a threat.

It would be easy to blame technology, and social media certainly plays a part. Yet the roots of the problem run deeper. People are living alone in greater numbers than ever, often in cities far from where they grew up. Traditional meeting places such as churches, unions and local clubs have lost members, and long working hours leave little time for friendship. Remote work, for all its advantages, has removed another source of casual daily contact. Contrary to the stereotype, surveys in several countries have found that young adults report feeling lonely more often than the elderly.

Importantly, loneliness is not the same as being alone. Many people live happily by themselves, while others feel deeply isolated in a crowded office or even a marriage. What matters is the gap between the relationships a person has and the ones they want. Loneliness is therefore subjective, which makes it hard to measure and easy to hide.

This distinction shapes the solutions. Simply putting people in the same room does little good; what helps is creating the conditions for meaningful connection. Some doctors now practise “social prescribing”, referring lonely patients to community gardens, choirs or volunteer groups rather than, or in addition to, prescribing medication. Early results suggest that such programmes reduce visits to the doctor, though larger studies are still needed. The idea is modest but powerful: shared activity can build the bonds that conversation alone often cannot.

puzzles.theme: Rewilding: Giving Land Back to Nature
puzzles.description: An article about rewilding and the environment: nature conservation, wolves, beavers and bison, farmers and rural communities.
text: In 1995, fourteen grey wolves were released into Yellowstone National Park in the United States, some seventy years after the species had been wiped out there. What followed has become one of the most famous stories in ecology. Deer and elk, no longer able to graze peacefully in open valleys, changed their behaviour. Vegetation along riverbanks recovered, birds and beavers returned, and the rivers themselves, some scientists argued, became more stable.

The story is often told as a neat fairy tale in which a single predator restored an entire ecosystem. The reality is messier. Later research has suggested that other factors, including hunting by humans, drought and the growing number of bears, also played important roles. Some ecologists now warn that the popular version may give the public unrealistic expectations. Nevertheless, Yellowstone helped to popularise an idea that is now reshaping conservation: rewilding.

Traditional conservation has often focused on protecting particular species or maintaining landscapes in a fixed state, sometimes through intensive management. Rewilding takes a different approach. Its supporters argue that, where possible, humans should step back and allow natural processes, such as flooding, grazing by large animals and the activity of predators, to shape the land. In Europe, projects have reintroduced bison to Romania, allowed wild horses and cattle to roam across former farmland in the Netherlands and restored beavers to rivers in Britain, where their dams can reduce flooding downstream.

Rewilding is not without controversy. Farmers worry, often with good reason, about wolves attacking livestock, and rural communities sometimes feel that decisions about their land are being made by urban environmentalists who will not live with the consequences. Critics also point out that European landscapes have been shaped by people for thousands of years, so it is far from obvious which past state should be restored.

The most successful projects seem to be those that treat local residents as partners rather than obstacles. In Portugal's Côa Valley, for instance, rewilding has been linked to new jobs in wildlife tourism, helping to slow the decline of villages that young people had been abandoning for decades. Compensation schemes for farmers who lose animals to predators have also reduced conflict in several countries.
Ultimately, rewilding asks a difficult question of a crowded continent: how much space are we willing to give back?

puzzles.description: An essay about advertising and marketing language: persuasion, weasel words, comparisons, brands and consumers.
text: Advertisers rarely lie outright. They do not need to. Over the past century, the industry has developed a sophisticated toolkit of linguistic techniques that allow it to suggest far more than it ever actually says, and most of us absorb these messages without noticing how they work.

One of the most effective tools is the so-called weasel word, a term that appears to make a strong claim while quietly emptying it of meaning. A shampoo that “helps reduce” dandruff has not promised to reduce it at all, only to contribute in some unspecified way. Products that fight “up to” 90% of germs may, legally speaking, fight far fewer. Phrases such as “clinically tested” sound scientific, yet say nothing about what the tests found.

Comparisons offer similar opportunities. A snack described as having “30% less fat” invites the question: less than what? The answer may be an unusually fatty original recipe or a competitor's product, but the missing half of the comparison is rarely supplied. Meanwhile, words like “natural”, “artisan” and “authentic” have become so common that they function less as descriptions than as moods, attaching a vague feeling of goodness to mass-produced goods.

Advertisers also exploit the way we process language emotionally. Brands increasingly address consumers as friends, adopting a casual, conversational tone and phrases such as “we've got you” or “treat yourself, you deserve it”. This intimacy is carefully engineered. By presenting a purchase as an act of self-care or identity, rather than a financial transaction, advertisers make it harder for us to evaluate the offer rationally. Children and teenagers, who are still developing critical reading skills, are particularly vulnerable to these techniques.

None of this is necessarily sinister. Persuasion is as old as language itself, and politicians, teachers and friends all choose their words strategically. Regulators in many countries also set limits: claims must generally be capable of being proven, and outright falsehoods can lead to fines. The difficulty is that much of the most powerful advertising language operates in the grey area between truth and deception, where it is technically accurate but designed to mislead.
The best defence, linguists suggest, is not cynicism but attention. Once you learn to notice a weasel word or an incomplete comparison, it is surprisingly difficult to stop seeing them everywhere.

puzzles.theme: Do Zoos Still Have a Place?
puzzles.description: An essay about zoos and animals: nature conservation, animal welfare, education, ethics and captivity.
text: For most of their history, zoos were little more than collections of exotic creatures displayed for public entertainment. Animals paced behind bars in concrete enclosures, and few visitors questioned whether this was acceptable. Today, the best zoos present themselves very differently: as centres of conservation, research and education. Critics, however, remain unconvinced that the change is more than cosmetic.

Supporters point to a number of genuine achievements. Several species that had disappeared from the wild, including the Arabian oryx and the California condor, survived thanks to breeding programmes in zoos and were later reintroduced into their natural habitats. Modern zoos also cooperate internationally to manage breeding and avoid the problems of inbreeding. In addition, they fund field projects, from protecting gorillas in Central Africa to monitoring coral reefs, and allow scientists to study animal behaviour and health in ways that would be difficult in the wild.

The educational argument is harder to assess. Zoos claim that seeing a living elephant inspires a lifelong concern for nature in a way that no documentary can. Yet studies measuring what visitors actually learn have produced mixed results, and many people spend only a few seconds at each enclosure before moving on to the café. Children, in particular, may remember the excitement of the day far better than any information about threats to wildlife.

The strongest objections concern welfare. Large, wide-ranging animals such as elephants, polar bears and orcas often struggle in captivity, where even spacious enclosures represent a tiny fraction of their natural territory. Some develop repetitive behaviours, such as swaying or pacing, which scientists regard as signs of stress. Moreover, only a minority of the species kept in zoos are actually endangered; many are there chiefly because they attract visitors.

A reasonable position may lie somewhere between abolition and complacency. Zoos could focus on species that genuinely benefit from captive breeding and that adapt well to life in enclosures, while gradually phasing out those that clearly suffer. Visitors, in turn, might have to accept seeing fewer charismatic animals. Such a transformation would be expensive and commercially risky, but if zoos are serious about their conservation mission, it may be the only way to justify their existence in the twenty-first century.

puzzles.description: An article about gamification: points, badges and game features in education, apps and work, motivation and learning.
text: Points for every workout, badges for finishing a language lesson, a daily streak that you would hate to break: game-like features have spread far beyond video games. Banks reward customers for saving, companies rank employees on leaderboards, and schools turn revision into competitions. This trend, known as gamification, promises to make dull or difficult activities more engaging. The question is whether it genuinely motivates people or merely keeps them busy.

There is good evidence that well-designed game elements can help. Clear goals, immediate feedback and a sense of progress are powerful motivators, which is why a progress bar that fills up as you complete a task can be surprisingly effective. Games also make failure less frightening, since losing a round simply means trying again. In education, several studies have found that quizzes with points and instant feedback improve both participation and memory, particularly for students who find traditional revision tedious.

The problems begin when the rewards become more important than the activity itself. Psychologists have long warned about what is sometimes called the overjustification effect: when people are rewarded for doing something they already enjoy, their natural interest can decline, because the activity starts to feel like a means to an end. A child who loves reading may read less once reading earns stickers, and stop altogether when the stickers disappear.

There is also a risk of manipulation. Many apps use techniques borrowed from gambling, such as unpredictable rewards and streaks that punish users for missing a single day, not to help people learn or stay healthy but to maximise the time they spend on the platform. In the workplace, public leaderboards can motivate the top performers while demoralising everyone else, and may encourage people to chase measurable targets at the expense of quality.

None of this means gamification is inherently harmful. Its effects depend on design and purpose. The most successful examples tend to support an activity that people already value, such as learning a language, rather than replacing that value with points. A good game element should work like scaffolding on a building: useful while it is needed, but never mistaken for the building itself. Before adding points to anything, designers, teachers and managers would do well to ask a simple question: what behaviour are we actually rewarding?

puzzles.description: An article about endangered languages: language death, culture, identity, globalisation and language revival.
text: Of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken in the world today, linguists estimate that around 40% are endangered. Many have only a few hundred speakers, most of them elderly. When the last fluent speaker of a language dies, something is lost that cannot be recovered from a dictionary: a unique way of describing the world, along with the songs, stories and knowledge that were passed down through it.

Languages have always risen and fallen, but the current rate of loss is unusually rapid. The causes are rarely mysterious. Economic migration draws young people to cities where a dominant language is essential for work. Schools and the media operate in national or global languages. Crucially, parents often choose not to pass on a minority language, believing that it will hold their children back. In many cases, this belief was reinforced by past policies that punished children for speaking their native language at school.

Why should anyone outside these communities care? One argument is scientific. Languages encode knowledge in ways that are easy to overlook: some indigenous languages contain precise vocabulary for local plants, animals and weather patterns that has proved valuable to biologists and ecologists. Another is cultural. For many communities, language is inseparable from identity, and its loss is often associated with a sense of disconnection from the past. Some researchers also suggest that speaking more than one language may bring cognitive benefits, although this remains debated.

Yet language death is not always irreversible. Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in religious texts, was revived as an everyday spoken language and today has millions of native speakers. Welsh, once in steep decline, has benefited from bilingual education and Welsh-language television, and in New Zealand, Māori ‘language nests’, in which preschool children are immersed in the language, have helped create a new generation of speakers.

Technology offers new tools as well. Communities are recording elders, creating apps and building online dictionaries, and social media has surprisingly become one of the places where young speakers use minority languages most. Such efforts, however, only succeed when people actually use the language in daily life. An archive can preserve a language in the way a museum preserves an extinct animal; it cannot make it live. That depends, ultimately, on whether speakers see their language not as a relic of the past but as part of their future.

puzzles.description: An article about lab-grown meat: food, science and technology, the environment, animal welfare, cost and consumers.
text: In 2013, a scientist in the Netherlands presented a hamburger that had cost more than 250,000 euros to produce. It had not come from a slaughtered cow but from cells grown in a laboratory. The tasters were polite rather than enthusiastic, but the event marked the beginning of an industry that its supporters believe could transform the way humanity eats.

The process, known as cultivated or lab-grown meat, involves taking a small sample of cells from a living animal and growing them in large steel tanks called bioreactors, where they are fed a nutrient-rich liquid. In principle, a single sample could produce enormous quantities of meat without raising or killing animals. In 2020, Singapore became the first country to approve the sale of cultivated meat.

The potential benefits are considerable. Livestock farming uses vast amounts of land and water and is responsible for a significant share of global greenhouse gas emissions. It is also a major driver of deforestation, including in the Amazon. Cultivated meat could, in theory, reduce all of these pressures while sparing billions of animals. Supporters also point out that meat produced in sterile conditions would be less likely to carry certain bacteria.

The obstacles, however, are just as considerable. Producing cultivated meat on an industrial scale remains extremely expensive, and some analysts doubt that costs can ever fall to the level of conventional meat. The environmental advantages are also less certain than they first appear: bioreactors require large amounts of energy, and if that energy comes from fossil fuels, the climate benefits could be small. Moreover, most products so far have imitated minced meat; recreating the complex structure of a steak is far harder.

Then there is the question of acceptance. Surveys suggest that many consumers are curious but uneasy about eating something produced in a factory, and farmers' organisations have campaigned for restrictions, arguing that the products should not even be allowed to use the word ‘meat’. Some places, including Italy, have gone further and banned its production and sale.

Whether cultivated meat becomes a staple or remains a curiosity may depend less on science than on price, energy and trust. For now, the most effective way to reduce the impact of meat remains the least technological: eating less of it.

puzzles.description: An essay on the psychology and economics of choice: shopping, consumer society, decisions, regret and happiness.
text: Walk into a large supermarket and you may find more than forty varieties of toothpaste, each promising whiter teeth, fresher breath or gentler care for sensitive gums. Few people would describe this abundance as a problem. Choice, after all, is closely bound up with freedom, and the ability to select precisely what suits us is often held up as one of the great achievements of consumer society. Yet a substantial body of research suggests that, beyond a certain point, more options can leave us less satisfied rather than more.

The idea gained wide attention through a now-famous experiment conducted in an upmarket Californian grocery store. On some days, shoppers were offered a tasting table with twenty-four varieties of jam; on others, just six. The larger display attracted more curious visitors, but those who saw the smaller selection were roughly ten times more likely to actually buy a jar. Faced with too many alternatives, the researchers concluded, people tend to defer the decision altogether.

The psychologist Barry Schwartz, whose book The Paradox of Choice popularised such findings, argued that the costs of abundance go beyond indecision. The more options we reject, the more we are haunted by the thought that one of them might have been better, so that even a good choice feels tainted by regret. Expectations rise, too: when hundreds of possibilities are available, anything short of perfection seems like a personal failure, since the ideal option was surely out there somewhere. Schwartz drew a distinction between “maximisers”, who feel compelled to find the best possible option, and “satisficers”, who are content with one that is good enough. Perhaps counterintuitively, maximisers often make objectively better decisions yet report being less happy with them.

It would be a mistake, however, to treat the jam study as an unassailable law of human behaviour. Subsequent attempts to replicate it have produced inconsistent results, and a large review of the research concluded that the average effect of choice overload is close to zero. What seems to matter is context. Abundance is more likely to overwhelm us when we lack clear preferences, when the options are difficult to compare, or when we are pressed for time. An expert coffee drinker may relish a menu of thirty blends that would leave a novice paralysed.

These nuances matter, because the notion of choice overload has been enthusiastically adopted by businesses and policymakers alike. Retailers trim their product ranges; governments design pension schemes with sensible default options so that people who never make an active decision are not left worse off. Such measures can be genuinely helpful. But they also raise an uncomfortable question about who gets to decide which options are shown and which quietly disappear.

The lesson, then, is not that choice is bad, but that it has costs as well as benefits, and that those costs fall unevenly. For most everyday purchases, deliberately settling for “good enough” may be the wisest strategy of all.

puzzles.description: An essay about boredom, creativity and the mind: smartphones and technology, daydreaming, attention and mental health.
text: Not so long ago, boredom was an unavoidable feature of daily life. It lurked in doctors' waiting rooms, on long bus journeys and in the slow hours of childhood summers. Today it has been all but abolished, or so it seems. With a smartphone in every pocket, no pause need ever go unfilled: a queue becomes an opportunity to check the news, a short wait for the kettle a chance to scroll through a feed. We have become so efficient at eliminating boredom that we rarely stop to ask whether it was ever worth keeping.

There are reasons to think it was. Boredom is, in essence, a signal: an uncomfortable message from the mind that our current situation is failing to engage us. Like hunger or pain, it is unpleasant precisely because it is meant to prompt action. The question is what kind of action. Reaching for a phone silences the signal instantly, but in doing so it may also cut short the process that boredom was designed to set in motion, namely the search for something more meaningful to do.

A number of studies have explored this possibility. In one frequently cited experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately tedious task, copying numbers from a telephone directory, subsequently came up with more inventive uses for a pair of plastic cups than those who had skipped the dull activity. The researchers suggested that boredom encourages the mind to wander, and that daydreaming allows loosely related ideas to collide in ways that focused thought does not. The findings are modest, and not every attempt to reproduce them has succeeded, but they chime with the testimony of countless writers and scientists who report that their best ideas arrived while they were walking, showering or staring out of a window.

None of this is to romanticise tedium. Chronic boredom, particularly in monotonous jobs or in institutions such as prisons, is associated with depression, risk-taking and addiction; it is a symptom of deprivation rather than a gateway to creativity. The boredom worth defending is the mild, temporary kind: the empty afternoon, the unscheduled half-hour, the moment of restlessness that precedes an idea.

Paradoxically, the technology that promises to rescue us from boredom may be making it harder to bear. Because stimulation is always available, our tolerance for its absence appears to be declining. In a series of experiments at the University of Virginia, many participants left alone in a room for up to fifteen minutes chose to give themselves mild electric shocks rather than sit quietly with their thoughts. The result was widely reported as evidence that people cannot stand their own company, although the researchers themselves were more cautious in their interpretation.

Reclaiming boredom need not involve renouncing technology. It may simply mean leaving the phone in a pocket during a commute, allowing children the occasional aimless afternoon, or resisting the urge to fill every silence. The discomfort will not disappear. But on the other side of it, there may be something we have been missing.

options: To argue that mild boredom has a value that constant stimulation may take away
To show that smartphones cause depression
To persuade readers to give up technology completely

questions.explain: The essay defends mild, temporary boredom as a signal that can lead to creativity, and suggests leaving room for it.

puzzles.description: An article about technology, law and justice: algorithms in courts, crime risk scores, bias, fairness and transparency.
text: In courtrooms across the United States, a defendant's future may be shaped not only by a judge and jury but by a piece of software. Risk-assessment algorithms, which estimate the likelihood that a person will commit another crime, are used in several states to inform decisions about bail, sentencing and parole. Their supporters present them as a corrective to human fallibility. Judges, after all, are prone to fatigue, prejudice and inconsistency; one widely discussed (and since contested) study even suggested that parole boards grew markedly harsher as the time since their last meal break increased. A well-designed algorithm, the argument goes, applies the same criteria to everyone, every time.

The difficulty lies in that phrase “well-designed”. Algorithms of this kind learn from historical data, and historical data reflects historical practice. If certain neighbourhoods have been policed more intensively than others, their residents will appear more frequently in arrest records, regardless of whether they actually commit more crimes. A system trained on those records may then conclude that living in such a neighbourhood, or possessing characteristics associated with it, signals higher risk. The algorithm does not need to be told a defendant's race to reproduce racial disparities; proxies such as postcode, employment history or family background can do the work silently.

This concern moved from theory to public controversy in 2016, when the investigative newsroom ProPublica analysed a widely used tool known as COMPAS. Its journalists reported that Black defendants who did not go on to reoffend were almost twice as likely as white defendants to have been wrongly labelled high-risk. The company behind the software disputed the analysis, pointing out that its scores predicted reoffending with similar accuracy for both groups. Remarkably, both claims could be true at once. Statisticians subsequently demonstrated that, when two groups have different underlying rates of rearrest, it is mathematically impossible for a tool to satisfy every reasonable definition of fairness simultaneously. Choosing between them is not a technical question but a moral one.

Compounding the problem is opacity. Many risk-assessment tools are developed by private companies that treat their methods as trade secrets, which means that defendants may be unable to examine, let alone challenge, the reasoning behind a score that affects their liberty. Some courts have ruled that this is acceptable as long as the score is not the only factor considered, a position that critics regard as a convenient fiction. Even where the code is available, the complexity of some machine-learning models makes their outputs difficult for anyone, including their designers, to explain.

None of this necessarily argues for abandoning such tools. The relevant comparison is not between algorithms and some ideal of perfect justice, but between algorithms and the flawed human judgements they supplement. What it does suggest is that their use demands transparency, independent auditing and a clear understanding that a score is an input to judgement, not a substitute for it. Delegating a decision to a machine does not remove the responsibility for its consequences; it merely makes that responsibility easier to overlook.

options: Risk-assessment algorithms raise serious problems of fairness and transparency that demand careful oversight

questions.explain: The writer does not call for abandoning the tools, but argues that bias, conflicting definitions of fairness and opacity require transparency and auditing.

questions.explain: A proxy represents something else. Postcode, for example, can indirectly represent race.

puzzles.description: An essay about translation, language and literature: untranslatable words, humour, faithful versus free translation and machine translation.
text: There is an old Italian pun, traduttore, traditore, which translates, rather neatly, as “translator, traitor”. The phrase captures a suspicion that has followed translators for centuries: that in carrying a text from one language to another, they inevitably betray it. Readers of translated fiction are frequently reminded of what they are missing, from untranslatable words to puns, rhythms and cultural references that simply do not survive the journey. Yet the image of translation as a process of loss, however persuasive, tells only part of the story.

Certainly, some things resist transfer. Portuguese speakers often point to saudade, a bittersweet longing for something absent, as a word with no English equivalent, and every language has its share of such treasures. But the existence of a single-word gap does not mean that the underlying experience cannot be conveyed. English speakers are perfectly capable of feeling saudade; they simply need more words, or a well-chosen image, to express it. Literary translators rarely work at the level of the individual word in any case. Their task is to recreate the effect of a sentence, a paragraph or a whole book, and this sometimes requires departing quite radically from the literal meaning.

Consider humour. A joke that depends on a double meaning in the original will fall flat if rendered word for word. The translator must either find a comparable pun in the target language, which may alter the content of the joke entirely, or sacrifice the wordplay and compensate elsewhere, perhaps by introducing a play on words a few lines later where the original had none. Purists may object that such choices take liberties with the author's work. Translators tend to reply that a literal version which fails to amuse is the greater betrayal.

Some of the most celebrated translations have arguably enriched their originals. The Persian poetry of Omar Khayyam became a Victorian bestseller in Edward FitzGerald's loose adaptation, which introduced it to millions of readers who would otherwise never have encountered it, even if scholars have long debated how faithful it really is. Writers themselves are often more relaxed about translation than their readers. The Portuguese novelist José Saramago reportedly remarked that writers make national literature, while translators make universal literature.

Recent advances in machine translation have given these debates new urgency. Automated tools can now render everyday prose with impressive fluency, and for many practical purposes they are more than adequate. Literary translation, however, depends on judgements about tone, ambiguity and cultural resonance that remain difficult to automate, not least because they are matters of interpretation rather than fact. Two skilled human translators will rarely produce identical versions of the same poem, and that variety is not a flaw to be engineered away but evidence of how much reading is itself an act of creation.

Perhaps, then, translation is better understood not as a copy that falls short of the original but as a new performance of it, in the way a piece of music is played differently by each musician. Something is always lost. But something, too, is always found.

puzzles.description: An article about economics, money and happiness: income, wellbeing, the Easterlin paradox, spending and how to measure a nation's progress.
text: For much of the twentieth century, economic growth was treated as a reliable proxy for human progress. If a country's gross domestic product was rising, its citizens were presumed to be getting better off, not merely in material terms but in their overall quality of life. In 1974, the economist Richard Easterlin published a paper that complicated this assumption. Within any given country, he found, richer people tended to report greater happiness than poorer ones. Yet over time, as national incomes rose substantially, average levels of reported happiness barely changed.

This apparent contradiction, which became known as the Easterlin paradox, has been debated ever since. One influential explanation emphasises comparison. If what matters to people is not their absolute income but their position relative to others, then a general rise in prosperity leaves everyone's relative standing unchanged, and satisfaction stays flat. A second explanation points to adaptation: we quickly grow accustomed to improvements in our circumstances, so that a larger house or a faster car delivers a burst of pleasure that soon fades into the new normal. Psychologists have memorably described this as a “hedonic treadmill”, on which we must keep running simply to stay in the same place.

Not everyone accepts the paradox. Using larger data sets covering more countries, later economists have argued that there is in fact a clear relationship between income and life satisfaction, both within and between nations, and that it does not disappear at higher incomes. Part of the disagreement stems from what exactly is being measured. Surveys that ask people to evaluate their lives as a whole tend to show satisfaction continuing to rise with income, whereas measures of day-to-day emotional experience, such as how often people feel joy or stress, level off more readily. A widely cited 2010 study suggested that emotional well-being stopped improving above an annual income of around 75,000 dollars, though a subsequent analysis found that for most people, happiness kept increasing well beyond that figure.

What seems less contested is that the way money is spent matters as much as how much of it there is. Research suggests that spending on experiences tends to bring more lasting satisfaction than spending on possessions, perhaps because experiences become part of our identity and are less easily compared with those of others. Spending money on other people, whether through gifts or charitable donations, also appears to produce greater happiness than spending the same amount on oneself. And buying time, by paying someone to do disliked chores, for instance, has been linked to lower stress.

Such findings have encouraged a number of governments to supplement GDP with broader measures of national well-being. Critics warn that happiness is too subjective and too easily manipulated to guide policy. Its advocates respond that GDP, which counts spending on disaster clean-ups and prison construction as contributions to growth, is hardly a neutral measure either. Whichever side one takes, the debate has made it harder to assume that a richer society is automatically a happier one.

puzzles.theme: Museums and the Ethics of Memory
puzzles.description: An essay about art, culture and history: museums, colonial-era collections, returning objects to their countries and telling the past.
text: In November 2021, twenty-six royal treasures left a museum in Paris and returned to Benin, in West Africa, almost 130 years after French soldiers had carried them away from the palaces of the Kingdom of Dahomey. The ceremony was hailed as historic, yet the twenty-six objects represented only a tiny fraction of the African artefacts held in French public collections, estimated at around ninety thousand. The episode brought into sharp focus a question that museums across Europe and North America can no longer avoid: to whom does the past belong?

For much of their history, the great encyclopaedic museums understood themselves as custodians of universal heritage. By gathering objects from every civilisation under one roof, they argued, they allowed visitors to grasp the shared story of humanity, while protecting fragile treasures that might otherwise be damaged, sold or lost. This argument retains some force. Many objects have undoubtedly survived because they were conserved in well-funded institutions, and millions of people have encountered cultures they would never otherwise have known.

Critics, however, contend that the universalist ideal conveniently obscures the circumstances in which many collections were assembled. A significant proportion of the objects in question were acquired during periods of colonial rule, through military expeditions, coercive purchases or outright looting. To describe such objects as belonging to all humanity, they argue, is to erase the specific communities from which they were taken, many of which still regard them not as works of art but as sacred items, ancestors or records of their own history. Moreover, the claim that institutions in the countries of origin could not care for them has often proved to be outdated, if not patronising.

In recent years, the balance of opinion has shifted perceptibly. Several governments have commissioned reports on restitution, and some institutions have begun to return objects voluntarily or to agree long-term loans. Others remain constrained by national laws that forbid the permanent removal of items from public collections, or by the practical difficulty of establishing the rightful recipient when the original owners were kingdoms or communities that no longer exist in their earlier form.

Restitution, though, is only part of the picture. A growing number of curators argue that museums must also change how they tell stories about the objects that remain. Labels that once described artefacts purely in terms of style and date now increasingly acknowledge how they came to be in the collection. Some exhibitions are developed jointly with representatives of source communities, whose knowledge can transform an object from an anonymous specimen into something with a name, a purpose and a living meaning.

None of these approaches offers a tidy resolution. But the debate has made one thing clear: a museum is never simply a neutral container for the past. The decisions it makes about what to display, how to describe it and whether to keep it are themselves part of history, and future generations will judge them accordingly.

puzzles.description: An essay about trust in science and experts: society, the media, uncertainty, misinformation and democracy.
text: It has become fashionable to declare that we live in an age of distrust in expertise. Politicians dismiss economists, online influencers challenge doctors, and anyone with an internet connection can find an article contradicting almost any scientific consensus. Yet the picture is more complicated than the headlines suggest. Surveys in many countries show that scientists remain among the most trusted professions, comfortably ahead of journalists and far ahead of politicians, although trust varies sharply along political lines in some places. What has changed is less the level of trust than its fragility, and the ease with which it can be exploited.

Part of the difficulty lies in a misunderstanding of how science works. Research proceeds by trial, error and revision; conclusions are provisional and are expected to change as evidence accumulates. To scientists, this is a strength. To a public accustomed to certainty, however, a change in official advice can look like incompetence or even deception. During public health emergencies, when guidance must be issued quickly on the basis of incomplete information, this gap in expectations becomes especially damaging. Paradoxically, the more openly scientists admit uncertainty, the more vulnerable they can appear to those who wish to exploit it.

Experts have not always helped their own cause. When they speak with unwarranted confidence, stray beyond their field or appear indifferent to the practical consequences of their recommendations, they invite suspicion. The spectacular failure of most economists to anticipate the 2008 financial crisis, for instance, left a lasting dent in the profession's credibility. Nor is expertise ever entirely neutral: deciding what counts as an acceptable risk involves values as well as data, and people who feel their values have been ignored are unlikely to be persuaded by statistics alone.

At the same time, the alternative to trusting experts is not independent thought but, in most cases, trusting someone else. No individual can personally verify the safety of a vaccine, the structural integrity of a bridge or the long-term effects of climate policy. We are all obliged to rely on others; the real question is how we choose whom to believe. Here, the philosopher Onora O'Neill has made a valuable distinction. Rather than asking whether people trust experts, she suggests, we should ask whether experts are trustworthy, and demand the kind of transparency that allows that judgement to be made intelligently.

This implies obligations on both sides. Experts need to communicate uncertainty honestly, explain how conclusions were reached and acknowledge the limits of their knowledge, even when a simpler message might seem more persuasive. Citizens, meanwhile, need enough scientific literacy to understand that disagreement at the frontiers of research does not mean that everything is up for debate. Schools have a role to play here, teaching not only scientific facts but how evidence is weighed. Doubt, after all, is at the heart of science. The problem arises only when it is detached from evidence and becomes a weapon rather than a method.

puzzles.description: An article about gene editing and CRISPR: science, medicine, genetic diseases, ethics, inequality and the future.
text: For most of history, the genetic code of living things could be read only with great difficulty and altered hardly at all. That changed dramatically in 2012, when Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier published research showing how a bacterial defence system known as CRISPR could be adapted to cut DNA at precisely chosen locations. The technique was cheaper, faster and more accurate than anything that had come before, and in 2020 it earned the two scientists the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The medical promise is extraordinary. In 2023, regulators in the United Kingdom and the United States approved the first CRISPR-based treatment, for sickle cell disease, a painful inherited blood disorder. Patients' own stem cells are removed, edited in the laboratory and returned to the body, where they begin producing healthy blood cells. The treatment, however, currently costs well over a million dollars per patient. Researchers are exploring similar approaches for certain cancers, inherited blindness and high cholesterol. For families who have watched generations suffer from the same condition, such developments can feel almost miraculous.

Yet the same technology raises some of the most profound ethical questions of our time. A crucial distinction separates somatic editing, which alters the cells of an individual patient, from germline editing, which alters embryos, eggs or sperm. Changes of the second kind would be inherited by future generations, who obviously cannot consent to them. When a Chinese scientist announced in 2018 that he had edited the genes of twin girls in an attempt to make them resistant to HIV, the reaction from the scientific community was almost universally hostile, and he was later sentenced to prison.

Opponents of germline editing warn of a slippery slope. Once it becomes acceptable to eliminate a devastating disease, they argue, the line between treatment and enhancement may prove impossible to hold. Wealthy parents might one day select embryos for height, intelligence or athletic ability, deepening existing inequalities and creating a society in which disadvantage is written into biology itself. Disability rights advocates add a further concern: that efforts to ‘correct’ certain conditions may imply that the lives of people who have them are less valuable.

Defenders respond that refusing to prevent serious suffering also carries moral weight, and that fears of designer babies overstate what genetics can achieve, since most complex traits depend on hundreds of genes and on environment. Off-target effects, in which the tool cuts DNA in unintended places, also remain a genuine technical risk. Many scientists therefore favour a cautious middle path: continuing research on somatic therapies while maintaining strict limits on germline applications until safety and social consensus are far clearer.

What is certain is that the decisions cannot be left to laboratories alone. The power to rewrite the code of life is too consequential to be governed by technical feasibility; it demands a public conversation about what kind of future we actually want. International bodies have called for such a conversation, but agreement across different cultures and legal systems will not come easily.
